title: ऋतुविचार खण्डकाव्यमा मोक्षचिन्तन {Mokshachintan in Rituvichara Khandakavya}
nepali: प्रस्तुत लेखमा लेखनाथ पौड्यालद्वारा रचित ऋतुविचार खण्डकाव्यलाई पौरस्त्य आध्यात्मिक दर्शनका मोक्षसम्बन्धी सैद्धान्तिक स्थापनाका आधारमा विवेचना गरिएको छ । विवेचनाका लागि आवश्यक सामग्रीको सङ्कलनका निम्ति पुस्तकालयीय सामग्री सङ्कलन विधिको प्रयोग गरिएको छ । यस सन्दर्भमा मोक्षसम्बन्धी सिद्धान्तको गहिराइको बोध गर्नका निम्ति क्रमशः उपनिषद्, साङ्ख्य, योग, न्याय, वैशेषिक, मीमांसा, वेदान्त र बौद्ध दर्शनका मोक्षसम्बन्धी स्थापनाहरूको अनुशीलन गरीमोक्ष भनेको के हो ? भन्ने कुरा प्रस्ट पारिएको छ । उपर्युक्त सबै दर्शनले मोक्षमाथि प्रकाश पार्ने प्रयत्न गर्दा प्रयोग गरिएका पद, पदावली, उपमान आदिका साथै अभिव्यक्तिको पद्धतिमा केही भिन्नता भए पनि सङ्केत गर्न खोजिएको कुरा एउटै भएको तथा यसलाई स्वयं अपरोक्षानुभूति नगरेसम्म पूर्ण रूपमा ज्ञात नहुने र अपरोक्षानुभूतिपछि पनि पूर्णरूपमा निर्वचनीय नरहेको कुरा प्रस्ट पारिएको छ । त्यसपछि ऋतुविचार खण्डकाव्यको सूक्ष्मपठन गरेर मोक्षसम्बन्धी चिन्तन अभिव्यञ्जित केही प्रमुख श्लोकहरू ठम्याई पौरस्त्य आध्यात्मिक दर्शनको केन्द्रविन्दुका रूपमा रहेको मोक्षसम्बन्धी सैद्धान्तिक स्थापनाका आधारमा विवेचना गर्दै खण्डकाव्यमा विषयगत विम्बहरूका रूपमा पूर्वीय दर्शनका मोक्षसम्बन्धी बिम्बहरू प्रशस्त प्रयोग भएकाले खण्डकाव्यका विभिन्न अंशमा मोक्षचिन्तन पनि कलात्मक उपकरणका रूपमा प्रभावकारी रूपमा आएको निचोड दिइएको छ ।
american_english: In this article, the khandakavya poem Rituvichara, composed by Lekhnath Paudyal, is examined on the basis of theoretical tenets concerning liberation (moksha) in Eastern spiritual philosophy. A library-based data collection method was utilized to gather the materials required for the discussion. In this context, in order to apprehend the depth of the doctrine of moksha, the positions regarding moksha across the Upanishads, Samkhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa, Vedanta, and Buddhist philosophies were investigated successively, clarifying the question of what moksha is. It is clarified that even though slight differences exist in the words, phrases, analogies, and modes of expression utilized when all the above philosophies attempt to illuminate moksha, the entity they seek to indicate is one and the same, and that it cannot be fully known until personally realized through direct perception (aparokshanubhuti), nor can it be completely expressed in words even after direct perception. Thereafter, conducting a close reading of the khandakavya Rituvichara, identifying certain key verses expressing thought on moksha, and evaluating them on the basis of theoretical tenets regarding moksha as the focal point of Eastern spiritual philosophy, the conclusion is offered that since motifs of moksha from Eastern philosophy are abundantly used as thematic imagery in the khandakavya, thought on moksha also emerges effectively as an artistic device throughout various sections of the poem.
british_english: In the present article, the khandakavya poem Rituvichara, composed by Lekhnath Paudyal, is analysed on the basis of theoretical propositions concerning liberation (moksha) in Eastern spiritual philosophy. A library-based material gathering method has been employed to assemble the materials required for the analysis. In this connection, to grasp the profound depth of the doctrine of moksha, the propositions concerning moksha in the Upanishads, Samkhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa, Vedanta and Buddhist philosophies were examined in turn, elucidating the question of what moksha is. It is elucidated that although certain variations exist in the vocabulary, phrasing, analogies and modes of expression employed when all the aforesaid philosophies attempt to throw light on moksha, what they endeavour to indicate is identical, and that it cannot be fully known until experienced directly through intuitive perception (aparokshanubhuti), nor is it entirely expressible even after such direct perception. Subsequently, through a close reading of the khandakavya Rituvichara, identifying several prominent verses expressing thought on moksha, and examining them on the basis of theoretical propositions regarding moksha as the core of Eastern spiritual philosophy, the conclusion is given that because imagery of moksha from Eastern philosophy is profusely used as thematic imagery within the khandakavya, thought on moksha also features effectively as an artistic device across different portions of the poem.
australian_english: In this paper, the khandakavya poem Rituvichara, written by Lekhnath Paudyal, is examined on the basis of theoretical tenets regarding liberation (moksha) in Eastern spiritual philosophy. A library-based method of gathering material was used to bring together the resources needed for the critique. In this context, to get a handle on the depth of the theory of moksha, the stances on moksha across the Upanishads, Samkhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa, Vedanta and Buddhist philosophy were looked at one by one, making clear what moksha actually is. It is made clear that while there are some differences in the terms, phrases, analogies and ways of putting things across when all the above philosophies try to shed light on moksha, what they are pointing towards is the exact same thing, and that it cannot be fully known without direct personal experience (aparokshanubhuti), nor can it be fully put into words even after that direct experience. Following that, through a close reading of the khandakavya Rituvichara, picking out several main verses reflecting contemplation on moksha, and looking into them on the basis of theoretical tenets of moksha as the centrepiece of Eastern spiritual philosophy, the conclusion is reached that since imagery of moksha from Eastern philosophy is widely used as thematic imagery in the poem, contemplation on moksha also works effectively as an artistic device across various parts of the poem.
informal_english: This paper takes a good look at the khandakavya poem Rituvichara, written by Lekhnath Paudyal, testing it against the main ideas about spiritual liberation (moksha) in Eastern philosophy. A standard library-based digging-out method was used to gather up all the material needed for the breakdown. To really get your head around how deep this moksha business runs, the paper goes through the Upanishads, Samkhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa, Vedanta and Buddhist schools one by one, spelling out what moksha is actually supposed to be. It makes the point that even though each of these schools uses different words, phrases, comparisons and ways of putting it when trying to shine a light on moksha, they're all getting at the very same thing, and you can't properly know it at all unless you experience it directly for yourself (aparokshanubhuti), nor can you ever properly describe it even after you've had that direct experience. After that, having a close read through the khandakavya Rituvichara and picking out a few key verses dealing with moksha, the paper weighs them up against the central ideas of Eastern spiritual philosophy, wrapping up with the point that because Eastern philosophical images of moksha are used all over the place as themes in the poem, meditating on moksha works grand as an artistic device right through the piece.
translator_notes: Philosophical systems (darshanas: Upanishad, Samkhya, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa, Vedanta, Bauddha) and technical concepts like 'अपरोक्षानुभूति' (direct unmediated spiritual realization) and 'अनिर्वचनीय' (indescribable / inexpressible) are maintained faithfully across all five sentences in strict sequence.
